summary:
Niger is among the most hostile jurisdictions in its region for a trans visitor, and the legal position has hardened in two stages since the July 2023 coup. In March 2025 the military junta's Charter of Refoundation outlawed “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” in Article 25, the first explicit statutory-level prohibition of same-sex conduct in the country's history. The charter sets no penalties of its own and operates during the five-year transition it declared; a draft penal code circulating since 2023 proposed up to five years for same-sex conduct, twenty years for conducting, officiating or witnessing a same-sex marriage, and five years for participating in or financing homosexual organisations.

The prohibition is now carried in the penal code itself. A February 2026 revision criminalises “indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts” under article 390, punishable by five to ten years' imprisonment and fines of up to 100 million CFA francs; same-sex marriage under article 391 carries ten to twenty years; article 392 targets LGBTQIA+ associations. The same article reaches anyone who “artificially changes sex at birth”, and the offence also covers changing or attempting to change one's birth sex and public announcement of a same-sex relationship. Mitigating circumstances and suspended sentences are unavailable for these offences. The state news agency, Agence Nigérienne de Presse, reported the criminalisation in June 2026.

Article 390's drafting is broad enough that commentators read asexuality as captured among sanctionable conduct, and the law has been denounced by the Oxford Human Rights Hub as violating the human rights of intersex as well as LGBTQIA+ people. For a trans visitor the operative risk is the sex-change clause: on its face it exposes a person who has changed, or attempted to change, recorded sex at birth to five to ten years' imprisonment, independent of any partner or conduct.

Enforcement since the 2026 code has been sweeping. The Guardian reported on 1 July 2026 that at least 40 people had been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, imprisoned across the country; campaigners described a witch-hunt in a toxic climate, and local media carried dozens of arrest reports. LGBTQIA+ people have gone into hiding, and organisations providing HIV prevention services to men who have sex with men stopped working after the law, cutting off access to condoms, HIV testing and PrEP and raising fears of an HIV resurgence.

Prosecution for same-sex conduct predates the 2025–26 statutes and has repeatedly been used through public-indecency provisions. In 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under article 276, which carried up to three years; the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them. In Niamey in 2025 two women reported by a third party were prosecuted for public indecency and acquitted because the facts did not pertain to the public sphere, and the judge was allegedly sanctioned for leniency. In Maradi in 2022 two young women were acquitted of lesbianism because no legislation then criminalised it, but were imprisoned for two years for posting nude videos allegedly portraying a lesbian act. Weeks after that acquittal, in December 2022, lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships.

Official hostility is stated openly. Justice Minister Alio Daouda said “all LGBTQ practices, whatever they may be” are “not in line with our social and cultural values”, and President Mohamed Bazoum's 2023 proposals framed the issue in public discourse as “social contagion”. Under the pre-2025 rules the age of consent was unequal, at 13 for different-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts.

Niger has no broad legal protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The only comparable provision still in force is article 95 of Law 2022-59 on the Protection of Personal Data, which prohibits collecting or data revealing sexual orientation and is punishable by three months to five years' imprisonment and fines of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs; the law was published in June 2025. The single earlier protection, article 4 of Law 2015-36 on Illicit Trafficking of Migrants, was repealed in 2023 by presidential decree, with prior convictions and their effects expunged.

Refugee and asylum claims by LGBTQIA+ people have failed. Asylum seekers from Cameroon, Liberia and Côte d'Ivoire who staged Niger's first LGBTQ public demonstration in Niamey in 2022 faced discrimination including shops refusing to serve them and verbal or physical violence from strangers, and the authorities refused to recognise their refugee status.
tangentialFactors:
Niger's 2025–26 measures sit within a wider pattern of states across one region hardening anti-LGBTQIA+ legislation, a framing used by El Espectador in July 2026; the direction of travel is restrictive rather than exceptional.

Reporting on violence has historically been suppressed rather than absent. The United States State Department's 2013 Human Rights Report found no reports of violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity and no documented discrimination, while cautioning that stigma or intimidation probably kept incidents unreported; the same report recorded two men caught naked in a parked car arrested and fined for public indecency, and found no documented discrimination in education under the same caveat. Absence of recorded incidents should not be read as absence of risk.

Societal stigma is documented independently of the statutes: LGBTQIA+ people in Niger face stigmatisation in the broader population, and historically many led socially acceptable public lives while keeping relationships private. The shift since 2026 is that this private accommodation no longer holds, with people going into hiding.

The collapse of HIV prevention services is a health consequence of the criminalisation regime rather than a separate policy, and campaigners interviewed in July 2026 warned of a resurgence as PrEP access fails.
localsOnly:
Article 392 of the February 2026 penal code punishes creating, managing, financing or participating in LGBTQIA+ organisations, clubs and social venues, directly or indirectly, with ten to twenty years' imprisonment and fines of up to 500 million CFA francs (about €762,244 / US$882,829). Two gay rights organisations reportedly operated in secret in Niger, partly because they were not formally registered, and organisations serving men who have sex with men ceased operating after the 2026 law.

Article 95 of Law 2022-59 on the Protection of Personal Data, published by the Ministry of Communication and New Information Technologies in June 2025, prohibits the collection or processing of data revealing sexual orientation, with penalties of three months to five years' imprisonment and fines of 5,000,000 to 50,000,000 CFA francs. It is the only anti-discrimination-adjacent protection still in force; article 4 of Law 2015-36 on Illicit Trafficking of Migrants was repealed in 2023 by decree of President Abdourahamane Tiani, with prior convictions and their effects expunged.

Residents face an unequal age of consent under the pre-2025 framework, at 13 for different-sex acts and 21 for same-sex acts, and the 2026 code removes mitigation and suspended sentences for the new offences. Public statements by Justice Minister Alio Daouda and the framing of “social contagion” in President Mohamed Bazoum's 2023 proposals indicate that official framing is aligned against LGBTQIA+ people rather than merely enforcing the text.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not establish how article 390's clause on “artificially chang[ing] sex at birth” has been applied in practice, whether it reaches persons who have changed official documents, or whether any court has interpreted it since February 2026. No sourced case law is available.

Unresolved: whether Article 25 of the Charter of Refoundation carries penalties of its own, or operates only through the penal code, is not settled in the sources; the Outright International overview states that no specific penalties were set at charter level.

Unresolved: the reading that the 2026 code captures asexuality rests on an interpretation of broad and inconsistent drafting by El Espectador, not on a judicial construction.

Unresolved: the figures of at least 40 arrests and 16 imprisonments, including military officials, come from a single July 2026 report and are not independently corroborated in the inventory; the scale of the round-up is therefore approximate.

Not sourced: the inventory contains nothing on legal gender marker or passport rules for trans visitors, on entry or visa screening that could reveal gender history, on access to gender-affirming care, or on facilities and bathroom rules. These are gaps in the record, not findings of safety.
